rv.q: What shocks in the end is that a play — yes, a play — that can, through its 80-minute running time, seem to de-prioritize plot for the poetic, also can conclude with an emotional wallop only a great playwright could produce, and only a stone could ignore.
Abraham’s production has the benefit of a truly lovely central performance from Price, a guileless and charming piece of acting that infuses the show with both honesty and courage.
As debuts go, this one's a triumph.

Sarah Ruhl’s play has aged well and it’s exciting to see one of her earlier works done to such incredible standards at a theater not far from where she grew up.
Bizarre as all these characters are, and how strange their circumstances, all is gloriously humorous.

cn.t: Critics praise this visually exquisite and emotionally resonant production, calling it a captivating revival that showcases new artistic director Braden Abraham's promising vision through poetic storytelling and elegant design.
